title: WhatsApp API Setup, Pricing and Limits for Developers
summary: WhatsApp API sends messages programmatically through Meta's platform. You'll know what access credentials and setup steps are needed to get started.
body_markdown:
## Call WhatsApp endpoints without code in Activepieces


You can send WhatsApp templates and receive replies without writing code in Activepieces, an open-source automation tool with an MIT-licensed core and 750 integrations, so you can almost certainly connect it to whatever other systems your business already uses.


It doesn't remove the Meta setup: the business account, phone number, template approval and messaging limits still sit with you.


Inside a flow, a rejected template or a degraded quality rating fails exactly as it does in a script, and the person paged will be whoever owns that flow.


### What the connector covers


Through the WhatsApp Business Platform, the Activepieces connector, one of the 750 integrations counted in the open source monorepo, sends text messages and template messages.


Before you build anything, you supply it with credentials from your own Meta account, so the connection is only as healthy as that account.


Meta decides approved templates, pricing category and per-number limits; the connector only passes your request along.


To receive replies, you use a webhook trigger. You register the webhook URL that Activepieces gives you in your Meta app's webhook configuration, and each reply or status update then starts a run of the flow.


Every plan, including free, allows unlimited flows, so the reply flow never competes with your other automations for a flow allowance.


Back to the previous section's warning: template rejections come back as status updates, so a flow triggered by that webhook can route them to a separate alert instead of letting them pass unnoticed.


For endpoints the connector doesn't expose, an HTTP step calls the Graph API directly with your access token. You get the same reach as code, but you read the endpoint's documentation and handle its errors yourself.


### Example: template message from a form submission


A form submission starts an Activepieces flow, and the flow's send-template step delivers an approved template to the customer's phone. On Activepieces Cloud, a run costs 1 credit however many steps it has.


The customer's reply returns through a webhook trigger that starts a second flow, with an HTTP step beneath it for any follow-up call.


What to take from it is that there are two separate entry points, one outbound and one inbound, and each needs its own owner and its own failure alert.


The send step names a template by its approved name and language and fills its variables from the form fields.


If the template isn't approved, or the variable count doesn't match, the step fails, and that failure should notify a person rather than sit in the run history.


Handle opt-outs and route conversations to a human in the reply flow, since a reply opens a service window that your next message depends on.


On Monday, work through these in order:


1. Write down who owns the Meta business account and who owns each flow, by name.
2. Confirm the template you plan to send is approved, in the language you'll use.
3. Check your messaging limit and quality rating in Meta's dashboard before connecting anything.
4. Register the webhook and route status updates, including rejections, to an alert channel.
5. Add a failure notification to every send step.
6. Send one real message from a form submission and read the run end to end.
